#| cache: false

Simple random sampling is the simplest probability sampling design, and the
building block for all the designs in later chapters. A stratified sample is an
SRS within each stratum; a cluster sample is an SRS of clusters. This chapter
defines the design, derives its estimators and their standard errors, shows how
to build confidence intervals and choose the sample size, and checks the theory
by simulation. The material corresponds to Sections 2.3–2.6 and 2.8 of Lohr and
Sections 4.1–4.5 of Scheaffer et al.

## SRS and SRSWR {#sec-srs-design}

There are two versions of simple random sampling.

A **simple random sample with replacement (SRSWR)** of size $n$ from a
population of $N$ units can be thought of as $n$ independent draws of one unit,
each unit having probability $1/N$ on every draw. The same unit can be drawn
more than once.

A **simple random sample without replacement (SRS)** of size $n$ is selected so
that every possible subset of $n$ distinct units in the population has the same
probability of being the sample. There are $\binom{N}{n}$ such subsets, so
$$
P(\mathcal S) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n!\,(N-n)!}{N!}
$$
for every subset $\mathcal S$ of size $n$. Unless stated otherwise, "SRS" in this
book means sampling without replacement. In practice an SRS is drawn with
computer-generated random numbers; in R,

```{r srs-draw-example}
#| eval: false
sample(1:N, size = n)
```

returns the labels of $n$ distinct units chosen in this way.

@fig-srs-design illustrates an SRS of $n = 60$ from a synthetic population of
$N = 1000$ units. The design uses no information about the units other than their
labels, so the sampled units (red) are scattered at random over the population,
and their values cover its whole range.

```{r fig-srs-design}
#| cache: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "A simple random sample of $n = 60$ (red) from a synthetic population of $N = 1000$ units, listed in an arbitrary order. The dashed line is the population mean."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "85%"
plot_design_srs()
```

### Inclusion probabilities

To study which units end up in the sample, define the sample-membership indicator
$$
Z_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if unit } i \text{ is in the sample,} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$
The probability $\pi_i = P(Z_i = 1)$ is the **inclusion probability** of unit
$i$. If unit $i$ is in the sample, the other $n-1$ sampled units must come from
the remaining $N-1$ units, so
$$
\pi_i = P(Z_i=1) = \frac{\text{number of samples including unit } i}{\text{number of possible samples}}
 = \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n}{N}.
$$
Every unit has the same chance $n/N$ of being in the sample. The indicators
$Z_1, \ldots, Z_N$ are the only random quantities in design-based inference; we
use them in @sec-srs-randomization to prove the properties of the estimators.

## Estimators for Simple Random Sampling {#sec-srs-formulas}

Write $y_i$ for the value of unit $i$ in the population $U = \{1, \ldots, N\}$,
and
$$
\bar{y}_U = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i, \qquad
t = \sum_{i=1}^N y_i = N\bar{y}_U, \qquad
S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \bar{y}_U)^2
$$
for the population mean, total and variance. These are fixed, unknown numbers.

### Estimating the population mean

The natural estimator of $\bar y_U$ is the sample mean, and the natural estimator
of $S^2$ is the sample variance:
$$
\bar y = \frac1n \sum_{i \in \mathcal S} y_i = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i y_i,
\qquad
s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} (y_i - \bar y)^2 .
$$
The sample mean is unbiased for $\bar y_U$, and its variance is
$$
V(\bar{y}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{S^2}{n}
$$
(both are proved in @sec-srs-randomization). This is the familiar $S^2/n$ of
independent sampling, multiplied by the factor $1 - n/N$, the **finite population
correction** (fpc). Sampling without replacement removes units from the pool, so
the sample covers more of the population than independent draws would, and the
variance is smaller. When the sampling fraction $n/N$ is small, the fpc is close
to $1$ and can be ignored. When $n = N$, the sample is a census and
$V(\bar y) = 0$.

Since $s^2$ is unbiased for $S^2$ (also proved in @sec-srs-randomization),
replacing $S^2$ by $s^2$ gives an unbiased estimator of the variance. Its square
root is the **standard error**:
$$
\boxed{
\hat{V}(\bar{y}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{s^2}{n}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\bar y) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s^2}{n}} .}
$$

### Estimating the population total

Since $t = N\bar y_U$, the total is estimated by scaling up the sample mean:
$$
\boxed{
\hat{t} = N\bar{y}, \qquad
\hat{V}(\hat{t}) = N^2\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{s^2}{n}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat{t}) = N\,\mathrm{SE}(\bar{y}).}
$$

**Sampling weights.** The estimated total can also be written with **sampling
weights**. The sampling weight of a unit is the reciprocal of its inclusion
probability, $w_i = 1/\pi_i = N/n$, and
$$
\hat t = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} w_i y_i = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \frac{N}{n} y_i .
$$
Each sampled unit "represents" $N/n$ units of the population: itself and
$N/n - 1$ unsampled ones. In an SRS all weights are equal; in later chapters
(stratified, cluster and unequal-probability sampling) they are not, but the
weighted-sum form of $\hat t$ carries over.

### Coefficient of variation

The standard error is in the units of $y$. A scale-free measure of precision is
the **coefficient of variation** (CV), defined when $\bar y_U \ne 0$:
$$
\mathrm{CV}(\bar y) = \frac{\sqrt{V(\bar y)}}{E(\bar y)}
 = \sqrt{1-\frac nN}\ \frac{S}{\sqrt n\, \bar y_{U}},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\bar y) = \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\bar y)}{\bar y} .
$$
Because $\hat t = N\bar y$, the factor $N$ cancels and
$\mathrm{CV}(\hat t) = \mathrm{CV}(\bar y)$. A CV of 0.05 means the standard error
is 5% of the estimate, whatever the units of measurement.

### Estimating a proportion

Estimating a proportion is a special case of estimating a mean. Define $y_i=1$ if
unit $i$ has the characteristic of interest and $y_i=0$ otherwise. Then the
population proportion and the sample proportion are
$$
p = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \bar y_{U}, \qquad
\hat p = \frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} y_i = \bar y ,
$$
so $\hat p$ is unbiased for $p$. For a 0/1 variable $y_i^2 = y_i$, and the
variances simplify:
$$
S^2 = \frac{N}{N-1}\,p(1-p), \qquad
s^2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\,\hat p(1-\hat p).
$$
Substituting into the general formulas,
$$
V(\hat p) = \Big(\frac{N-n}{N-1}\Big)\frac{p(1-p)}{n},
\qquad
\boxed{\hat V(\hat p) = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{\hat p (1-\hat p)}{n-1}.}
$$
The number of units with the characteristic, $Np$, is estimated by $N\hat p$ with
standard error $N\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat p)$.

## Example: The Census of Agriculture {#sec-srs-agsrs}

The U.S. government conducts a Census of Agriculture every five years. It
collects data on all farms (any place producing \$1000 or more of agricultural
products) in the 50 states, for each of the $N=3078$ counties and
county-equivalents. The file `agpop.csv` contains the 1982, 1987 and 1992 farm
data for the whole population. An SRS of $n=300$ counties was selected with
computer-generated random numbers and saved as `agsrs.csv`. We use it to
estimate the mean and total of `acres92`, the number of acres devoted to farms
in 1992, and the proportion of counties with fewer than 200,000 acres in farms.

Throughout the agriculture examples in this book, county acreages are expressed
in **thousands of acres**. The raw figures run into the millions, and every
mean, variance and total reads far more easily on that scale. The helper
`acres_in_thousands()` performs the conversion as the data are read.

### Step-by-step calculation

We first compute the estimates directly from the formulas of @sec-srs-formulas.

```{r srs-manual-calc}
## read survey data
agsrs <- read.csv ("data/agsrs.csv")
## work in thousands of acres, the unit used for every agriculture example here
agsrs[c("acres92", "acres87", "acres82")] <- agsrs[c("acres92", "acres87", "acres82")] / 1000
head(agsrs)

## extract the variable of interest
sdata <- agsrs$acres92
N <- 3078

## do calculation
n <- length (sdata)
ybar <- mean (sdata)
s <- sd (sdata)
se.ybar <- sqrt((1 - n / N)) * s / sqrt(n)
mem <- qt (0.975, df = n - 1) * se.ybar

## return estimate vector for pop mean
c (Est. = ybar, S.E. = se.ybar, ci.low = ybar - mem, ci.upp = ybar + mem)

## return estimate vector for pop total
c (Est. = ybar, S.E. = se.ybar, ci.low = ybar - mem, ci.upp = ybar + mem) * N
```

In thousands of acres, the sample gives $\bar y = `r round(ybar, 3)`$ and
$s = `r round(s, 2)`$, so
$$
\mathrm{SE}(\bar y) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac{300}{3078}\Big)\frac{`r round(s, 2)`^2}{300}} = `r round(se.ybar, 3)`,
$$
$$
\hat t = N\bar y = 3078(`r round(ybar, 3)`) = `r format(round(N * ybar), big.mark = ",")`,
\qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat t) = 3078(`r round(se.ybar, 3)`) = `r format(round(N * se.ybar), big.mark = ",")` .
$$
The average county has about `r round(ybar)` thousand acres in farms, and the
U.S. total is estimated at about `r round(N * ybar / 1e3)` million acres. The
estimated coefficient of variation is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\hat t) = \widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\bar y)
 = \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\bar y)}{\bar y}
 = \frac{`r round(se.ybar, 3)`}{`r round(ybar, 3)`} = `r round(se.ybar / ybar, 4)`,
$$
so the standard error is about `r round(100 * se.ybar / ybar, 1)`% of the estimate.

The data are highly skewed (@fig-agsrs-acres92-hist): most counties have fewer
than 500 thousand acres in farms, but some have more than 1.5 million. For such
data the mean is pulled up by the long right tail, and we should also report the
**median**, which is `r round(median(sdata), 1)` thousand acres here, well below
the mean.

```{r fig-agsrs-acres92-hist}
#| fig-cap: "Farm acreage in 1992 (thousands of acres) for the SRS of 300 counties. The distribution is strongly skewed to the right."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
hist(sdata, breaks = 30, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
     xlab = "acres92 (thousands of acres)", main = "")
abline(v = c(ybar, median(sdata)), col = c("firebrick", "darkgreen"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2))
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), col = c("firebrick", "darkgreen"),
       legend = c("mean", "median"))
```

**A proportion.** Let $y_i = 1$ if county $i$ has fewer than 200 thousand acres
in farms. In the sample, `r sum(sdata < 200)` of the 300 counties do, so
$\hat p = `r sum(sdata < 200)`/300 = `r round(mean(sdata < 200), 2)`$ and
$$
\mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac{300}{3078}\Big)\frac{(`r round(mean(sdata < 200), 2)`)(`r round(1 - mean(sdata < 200), 2)`)}{299}} = `r round(sqrt((1 - n/N) * mean(sdata < 200) * (1 - mean(sdata < 200)) / (n - 1)), 4)` .
$$

### A function for repeated use

The same calculation is needed again and again, so we wrap it in a function. To
avoid repeating code in every chapter, all estimating functions (and their `gt`
table formatting helpers) live in a single shared file, `samplingestimate.r`,
sourced at the start of this chapter. The SRS function is `srs_est()`.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

<details>
<summary>Show the shared estimating functions (`samplingestimate.r`)</summary>

```{r print-functions}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("```r\n")
cat(readLines("samplingestimate.r"), sep = "\n")
cat("\n```\n")
```

</details>

:::

```{r agsrs-load}
agsrs <- acres_in_thousands (read.csv ("data/agsrs.csv"))
```

*Estimating the mean of acres92.* The function's `$table` shows the row-level
working values (the first 6 rows and the Sum), and `$estimate` holds the point
estimate, SE and CI, formatted with `format_est_gt()`.

```{r agsrs-mean-est}
res_mean <- srs_est(agsrs[,"acres92"], N = 3078, estimate = "mean")
res_mean$table
res_mean$estimate |> format_est_gt("mean")
```

*Estimating the total of acres92.* Setting `estimate = "total"` makes the
function scale the mean and confidence interval by $N = 3078$.

```{r agsrs-total-est}
res_total <- srs_est(agsrs[,"acres92"], N = 3078, estimate = "total", show.details = FALSE)
res_total$estimate |> format_est_gt("total")
```

*Estimating the proportion of counties with fewer than 200K acres.* We create the
0/1 indicator and estimate its mean.

```{r agsrs-prop-est}
acres92.is.fewer.200k <- as.numeric (agsrs[,"acres92"] < 200)   # 200 thousand acres
head(acres92.is.fewer.200k)

res_prop <- srs_est(acres92.is.fewer.200k, N = 3078, estimate = "mean", show.details = FALSE)
res_prop$estimate |> format_est_gt("mean")
```

*Estimating the number of such counties.*

```{r agsrs-prop-total-est}
res_prop_total <- srs_est(acres92.is.fewer.200k, N = 3078, estimate = "total", show.details = FALSE)
res_prop_total$estimate |> format_est_gt("total")
```

### Comparing with the true values

Because the census file `agpop.csv` contains the whole population, we can check
how close the SRS estimates came to the true values. (In a real survey these are,
of course, unknown.)

```{r agpop-true-values}
agpop <- acres_in_thousands (read.csv ("data/agpop.csv"))
#true mean (thousands of acres)
mean (agpop[, "acres92"], na.rm = T)
# true total (thousands of acres)
sum (agpop[, "acres92"], na.rm = T)

# true proportion of counties with less than 200K acres for farming
mean (agpop[, "acres92"] < 200, na.rm = T)
# true number of counties with less than 200K acres for farming
sum (agpop[, "acres92"] < 200, na.rm = T)
```

All the true values lie inside the 95% confidence intervals computed above.

## Confidence Intervals {#sec-srs-ci}

A confidence interval (CI) indicates the accuracy of an estimate. A 95% CI is
often explained heuristically: if we took samples from the population over and
over again, and constructed a CI by our procedure for each possible sample, we
would expect 95% of the resulting intervals to include the true value of the
population quantity. In design-based inference this is literally what the
probability refers to: the population is fixed and the randomness is over the
$\binom{N}{n}$ possible samples.

### Normality of the sample mean

In an SRS without replacement the observations are not independent, so the
ordinary central limit theorem does not apply directly. A finite-population
version is due to Hájek (1960): if certain technical conditions hold and $n$,
$N$ and $N-n$ are all "sufficiently large", then the sampling distribution of
$$
\frac{\bar y - \bar y_{U}}{\sqrt{\big(1-\tfrac nN\big)}\, \tfrac{S}{\sqrt n}}
$$
is approximately standard normal. Replacing $S$ by $s$ gives the standard error,
and approximate $100(1-\alpha)\%$ CIs for the mean, total and proportion are
$$
\bar y \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\bar y), \qquad
\hat t \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\hat t), \qquad
\hat p \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\hat p).
$$
The $t$ quantile is customary; for the sample sizes used in surveys it is very
close to the normal quantile $z_{\alpha/2}$.

**Example (continued).** For the agriculture sample,
$t_{0.025,\,299} = `r round(qt(0.975, 299), 3)`$, and the 95% CIs are
$$
\text{mean: } `r round(ybar, 1)` \pm `r round(qt(0.975, 299), 3)`(`r round(se.ybar, 2)`) = [`r round(ybar - mem, 1)`,\ `r round(ybar + mem, 1)`] \text{ thousand acres},
$$
$$
\text{total: } [`r format(round(N * (ybar - mem)), big.mark = ",")`,\ `r format(round(N * (ybar + mem)), big.mark = ",")`] \text{ thousand acres},
$$
$$
\text{proportion: } `r round(mean(sdata < 200), 2)` \pm `r round(qt(0.975, 299), 3)`(`r round(sqrt((1 - n/N) * mean(sdata < 200) * (1 - mean(sdata < 200)) / (n - 1)), 4)`) = [`r round(res_prop$estimate["ci.low"], 3)`,\ `r round(res_prop$estimate["ci.upp"], 3)`],
$$
matching the output of `srs_est()` in @sec-srs-agsrs.

### How large must $n$ be for normality?

The normal approximation needs a larger sample when the population is skewed,
as acreage is. Sugden, Smith and Jones (2000) extend Cochran's rule and
recommend the minimum sample size
$$
n_{\min} = 28 + 25\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\bar y_{U})^3}{N S^3}\right)^{\!2},
$$
where the quantity in parentheses is the **skewness** of the population. The
more skewed the population, the larger the sample required.

```{r srs-nmin}
g1 <- (sum((sdata - ybar)^3) / n) / s^3   # sample skewness
n_min <- 28 + 25 * g1^2
c(skewness = g1, n_min = n_min)
```

For the agriculture data we substitute the sample quantities: $s = `r round(s, 2)`$
and $\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^3/n = `r round(sum((sdata - ybar)^3) / n / 1e8, 4)` \times 10^{8}$
(in thousands of acres), giving a skewness of `r round(g1, 2)` and
$$
n_{\min} = 28 + 25(`r round(g1, 3)`)^2 \approx `r round(n_min)` .
$$
Our sample of $n=300$ exceeds $n_{\min}$, so it appears large enough for the
sampling distribution of $\bar y$ to be approximately normal. The simulation in
@sec-srs-simulation confirms this.

## Choosing the Sample Size {#sec-srs-sample-size}

Before a survey is carried out we must decide how large the sample should be.
The answer depends on how precise the estimate must be.

### Specifying the tolerable error

The desired precision is often expressed in absolute terms,
$$
P(|\bar y - \bar y_{U}| \le e) = 1-\alpha ,
$$
where $e$ is the **margin of error**. For many surveys of people that measure a
proportion, $e=0.03$ and $\alpha=0.05$. Alternatively, precision can be specified
in relative terms, which controls the CV:
$$
P\left(\left|\frac{\bar y - \bar y_{U}}{\bar y_{U}}\right| \le r\right) = 1-\alpha,
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad e = r \, \bar y_{U} .
$$
For example, if $\bar y_{U} \approx 180$ thousand and $r=0.1$, then $e=18$ thousand.

### Solving for $n$

Using the normal approximation, the margin of error is
$z_{\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SD}(\bar y)$, so we need $n$ with
$$
e = z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S^2}{n}} .
$$
Solving in two steps is convenient. First find the sample size $n_0$ we would
need for an infinite population (no fpc):
$$
n_0 = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\, S}{e}\right)^{\!2}.
$$
Then adjust for the finite population:
$$
\boxed{n = \frac{n_0}{1+n_0/N} = \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 S^2}{e^2 + z_{\alpha/2}^2 S^2/N}.}
$$
When $N$ is large relative to $n_0$, $n \approx n_0$; the population size
matters only when $n_0$ is a substantial fraction of $N$. The formula needs a
value for $S$, which is unknown. It can come from a pilot sample, a previous
survey of a similar population, or a guess. For a proportion,
$S^2 \approx p(1-p) \le 1/4$, so using $p = 1/2$ gives a conservative
(largest) sample size.

```{r srs-sample-size-fn}
srs_size <- function(S, e, N = Inf, alpha = 0.05) {
  n0 <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * S / e)^2
  c(n0 = n0, n = n0 / (1 + n0 / N))
}
```

**Example: margin of error 0.03 for a proportion.** We want to estimate the
proportion of the $N=1251$ recipes in a cookbook that do not involve animal
products, with a 95% CI of margin of error 0.03. Using the conservative
$p = 1/2$,
$$
n_0 = \frac{(1.96)^2 (\tfrac12)(1-\tfrac12)}{(0.03)^2} \approx 1067 .
$$
Since $n_0$ is large relative to $N=1251$, the fpc adjustment matters:
$$
n = \frac{n_0}{1+n_0/N} = \frac{1067}{1+1067/1251} \approx 576 .
$$
If $N$ were very large we would use $n\approx n_0 = 1067$.

```{r srs-size-cookbook}
srs_size(S = 0.5, e = 0.03, N = 1251)
```

**Example: the agriculture survey.** A pilot sample of 30 counties was taken
(one county was missing `acres92`). The sample SD of the remaining 29
observations was 519.085 thousand acres. With a desired margin of error of
60 thousand acres,
$$
n_0 = (1.96)^2\,\frac{519.085^2}{60^2} \approx 288,
\qquad
n = \frac{288}{1+288/3078} \approx 263 .
$$
The investigators took a sample of 300, in case the pilot's estimate of the SD
was too low.

```{r srs-size-agri}
srs_size(S = 519.085, e = 60, N = 3078)
```

## Randomization Theory for SRS {#sec-srs-randomization}

We now prove the properties of $\bar y$ and $s^2$ used above. In the
**randomization theory** (design-based) approach, the values $y_1, \ldots, y_N$
are fixed but unknown numbers. The only random variables are the indicators
$Z_1, \ldots, Z_N$ that record which units are in the sample:
$$
\bar y = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \frac{y_i}{n} = \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i \frac{y_i}{n} .
$$
All the randomness in $\bar y$ comes from $Z_1,\ldots,Z_N$.

### Moments of $Z_i$

Each $Z_i$ is a Bernoulli random variable with
$P(Z_i=1) = \pi_i = n/N$ (@sec-srs-design). Since $Z_i^2 = Z_i$,
$$
E[Z_i] = E[Z_i^2] = \frac nN, \qquad
V(Z_i) = \frac nN - \Big(\frac nN\Big)^2 = \frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big).
$$
The $Z_i$ are not independent, because the sample size is fixed: if unit $i$ is
in the sample, there is one less place for the other units. For $i\ne j$, given
that unit $i$ is sampled, the remaining $n-1$ units are an SRS from the other
$N-1$, so
$$
E[Z_iZ_j] = P(Z_j=1\mid Z_i=1)\,P(Z_i=1) = \frac{n-1}{N-1}\cdot\frac nN ,
$$
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j) = E[Z_iZ_j]-E[Z_i]E[Z_j]
 = \frac nN\Big(\frac{n-1}{N-1} - \frac nN\Big)
 = -\frac{1}{N-1}\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac nN .
$$
This **negative** covariance is the source of the finite population correction.

### Unbiasedness of $\bar y$

By linearity of expectation,
$$
E[\bar y] = \sum_{i=1}^N E[Z_i]\frac{y_i}{n}
 = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{n}{N}\cdot\frac{y_i}{n}
 = \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \bar y_{U}.
$$
So $\bar y$ is an **unbiased** estimator of $\bar y_{U}$, and $\hat t = N\bar y$ is
unbiased for $t$.

### Variance of $\bar y$

Expanding the variance of a sum,
$$
V(\bar y) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2\, V(Z_i) + \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j\ne i} y_i y_j\,\mathrm{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j)\right]
 = \frac{1}{n^2}\,\frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\left[\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2 - \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j\ne i} y_i y_j\right].
$$
Using $\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i} y_iy_j = \big(\sum_i y_i\big)^2 - \sum_i y_i^2$, the term
in brackets is
$$
\frac{N\sum_{i} y_i^2 - \big(\sum_{i} y_i\big)^2}{N-1}
 = \frac{N\sum_i (y_i - \bar y_U)^2}{N-1} = N S^2 .
$$
Therefore
$$
V(\bar y) = \frac{1}{n^2}\,\frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big) N S^2 = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S^2}{n}.
$$
Without the negative covariances, the result would be $\frac{N-1}{N}\cdot\frac{S^2}{n}$
(the SRSWR variance). The covariance terms produce the factor $1 - n/N$.

### Unbiasedness of $s^2$

Adding and subtracting $\bar y_U$ inside the sum of squares gives the identity
$$
\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^2 = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y_{U})^2 - n(\bar y - \bar y_U)^2 .
$$
Take expectations. For the first term,
$E\big[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i(y_i-\bar y_U)^2\big] = \frac nN (N-1)S^2$; for the
second, $E[n(\bar y - \bar y_U)^2] = nV(\bar y) = (1-\frac nN)S^2$. Hence
$$
E\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^2\right]
 = \frac{n(N-1)}{N}S^2 - \frac{N-n}{N}S^2 = (n-1)S^2 ,
$$
and therefore $E[s^2] = S^2$. It follows that $\hat V(\bar y) = (1-\frac nN)\frac{s^2}{n}$
is unbiased for $V(\bar y)$. (The standard error, its square root, is slightly
biased, as a square root always is, but this is ignored in practice.)

## A Simulation Demonstration of SRS Inference {#sec-srs-simulation}

The theory says that $\bar y$ is unbiased, that its standard deviation is
$\sqrt{1-n/N}\,S/\sqrt n$, that it is approximately normal for $n = 300$, and
that the 95% CIs cover $\bar y_U$ about 95% of the time. Because `agpop.csv`
contains the whole population, we can check all four claims by drawing many
samples from it.

```{r agpop-load-clean}
#| code-fold: true
# read population data, with acreages in thousands of acres
agpop <- acres_in_thousands (read.csv ("data/agpop.csv"))
# remove those counties with na
agpop <- subset( agpop, !is.na (acres92))
```

### True values

We fix the sample size and compute the true population mean and the true
standard deviation of $\bar y$ from the population $S$:
$$
\mathrm{SD}(\bar{y}) = \sqrt{1 - \frac{n}{N}} \left(\frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
$$

```{r srs-true-values}
#| code-fold: true
# sample size
n <- 300
# population size
N <- nrow (agpop); N

# true value of population mean
ybarU <- mean (agpop[,"acres92"]); ybarU
# true value of deviation of sample mean
true.se.ybar <- sqrt (1- n/N) * sd (agpop[,"acres92"]) / sqrt (n); true.se.ybar
```

### One SRS

A single random sample of $n=300$, analyzed with `srs_est()`, is one instance of
survey inference:

```{r srs-one-sample}
#| code-fold: true
# srs sampling
srs <- sample (1:N,n)
head(agpop [srs, ])
# get data of variable "acres92"
sdata <- agpop [srs, "acres92"]
# analysis
res_one <- srs_est(sdata, N, estimate = "mean", show.details = FALSE)
res_one$estimate |> format_est_gt("mean")
```

### Repeating SRS 5000 times

We now draw 5000 independent samples and store the estimates from each. (We use
`show.details = FALSE` and keep only `$estimate`, so the loop skips building 5000
working tables.)

```{r fig-srs-simulation-distribution, fig.height=10}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Population distribution and sampling distribution of the SRS sample mean over 5000 repeated samples (n = 300)"
nres <- 5000 # number of repeated sampling
simulation.results <- matrix (0, nres, 4) # matrix recording repeated results
colnames(simulation.results) <- c( "Est.",   "S.E.",   "ci.low", "ci.upp")

for (i in 1:nres)
{
    srs <- sample (N, n)
   sdata <- agpop [srs, "acres92"]
   simulation.results [i,] <- srs_est (sdata, N, estimate = "mean", show.details = FALSE)$estimate
}

head(simulation.results)
# look at the distribution of sample mean
par (mfrow= c(2,2))
dens_pop <- density (agpop$acres92, from = 0)
hist (agpop$acres92, breaks = 50, freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
      ylim = c(0, max (dens_pop$y)),
      main = "Population of acres92", xlab = "acres92")
lines (dens_pop, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
hist (simulation.results[,1], breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
      main = "Sample means of acres92", xlab = "sample mean")
lines (density (simulation.results[,1]), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
curve (dnorm (x, mean = ybarU, sd = true.se.ybar), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline (v = ybarU, col = "red")
legend ("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), col = c("blue", "red"), cex = 0.8,
        legend = c("kernel density", "normal (theory)"))
qqnorm (simulation.results[,1], main="QQ plot of Sample Mean"); qqline(simulation.results[,1])
boxplot (simulation.results[,1], main = "Boxplot of Sample Mean")
abline (h = ybarU, col = "red")

mean (simulation.results[,1])
ybarU
sd (simulation.results [,1])
true.se.ybar
```

The blue curves are kernel density estimates. The population density (top left)
is strongly skewed to the right, with a long tail of very large counties. The
kernel density of the 5000 sample means (top right) is nearly symmetric and
almost coincides with the normal density $N\big(\bar y_U,\ \mathrm{SD}(\bar y)^2\big)$
predicted by the theory (red dashed curve); the QQ plot (bottom left) is close to
a straight line, with only a slight bend in the upper tail left over from the
skewness. So the sampling distribution of $\bar y$ is close to normal, as Hájek's theorem and
the $n_{\min}$ check of @sec-srs-ci suggest. The average of the 5000 estimates,
`r round(mean(simulation.results[,1]), 2)`, is close to $\bar y_U = `r round(ybarU, 2)`$
(unbiasedness), and their standard deviation,
`r round(sd(simulation.results[,1]), 2)`, is close to the theoretical value
`r round(true.se.ybar, 2)`.

### Empirical coverage rate of CIs

Finally we check whether the 95% CIs cover the true mean about 95% of the time.

```{r srs-coverage-setup}
#| code-fold: true
library(plotrix)

# Convert to data frame (if it was a matrix) and use mutate to evaluate coverage
simulation.results <- as.data.frame(simulation.results) |>
  mutate(
    `Covered?` = as.numeric(ci.low < ybarU & ybarU < ci.upp)
  )

head(simulation.results)
```

```{r fig-srs-coverage-intervals, fig.height=6}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "First 100 simulated 95% confidence intervals for the SRS sample mean, with coverage failures highlighted"
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
plotCI(
  x = 1:100,
  y = simulation.results$Est.[1:100],
  li = simulation.results$ci.low[1:100],
  ui = simulation.results$ci.upp[1:100],
  col = 2 - simulation.results$`Covered?`[1:100]
)
abline(h = ybarU, col = "blue")

# Empirical coverage rate
mean(simulation.results$`Covered?`)
```

The empirical coverage rate is `r round(mean(simulation.results$"Covered?"), 3)`,
close to the nominal 0.95. (With a skewed population the coverage of the
$t$ interval tends to fall slightly short of nominal.) The intervals that miss (in red) are exactly the
"5% of samples" in the heuristic interpretation of @sec-srs-ci.

## Shinylive App for Illustrating SRS Theory {#sec-app-srs}

The simulation for this section runs as a standalone app:
[Simple random sampling](../shinylives_sampling/app-srs.html){target="_blank"}.
It draws samples one at a time and builds up the sampling distribution and the
coverage rate interactively, for any sample size and confidence level. It opens
in a new tab, together with its documentation and the full
[list of apps](../shinylives_sampling/index.html){target="_blank"}.
